claim: There are approximately 50,000 reported cases of VL per year, with the vast majority of infections in South America, East Africa and the Indian subcontinent.
source: There are approximately 50,000 reported cases of VL per year, with the vast majority of infections in South America, East Africa and the Indian subcontinent.
evidence: This is a factual statement about VL epidemiology that draws from established knowledge in the field.

claim: The actual annual incidence of VL is estimated to be between 200,000 and 400,000 cases.
source: However, the number of cases is likely to be vastly underreported, with the actual annual incidence estimated to be between 200,000 and 400,000 (Alvar et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alvar et al., 2012.

claim: VL is fatal if untreated.
source: VL is fatal if untreated and, in the absence of effective vaccines and vector control methods, efficacious chemotherapy is required to combat the disease.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the natural history of VL.

claim: Each of the currently available VL drugs has one or more drawbacks, including the need for hospitalization, prolonged therapy, parenteral administration, high cost, variable efficacy, severe toxic side-effects and resistance.
source: Each of the currently available drugs has one or more drawbacks, including the need for hospitalization, prolonged therapy, parenteral administration, high cost, variable efficacy, severe toxic side-effects and resistance (Croft et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Croft et al., 2006.

claim: Fexinidazole was discovered to have potent activity in a murine VL model.
source: In addition, the anti-trypanosomal clinical candidate fexinidazole was recently discovered to have potent activity in a murine VL model (Wyllie et al., 2012), resulting in a phase II proof of concept clinical trial (NCT01980199) against VL being conducted in Sudan.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wyllie et al., 2012.

claim: A phase II proof of concept clinical trial (NCT01980199) against VL with fexinidazole is being conducted in Sudan.
source: In addition, the anti-trypanosomal clinical candidate fexinidazole was recently discovered to have potent activity in a murine VL model (Wyllie et al., 2012), resulting in a phase II proof of concept clinical trial (NCT01980199) against VL being conducted in Sudan.
evidence: This is a factual statement about a clinical trial with a specific identifier.

claim: (S)-PA-824 possesses moderate activity against L. donovani parasites both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Recently, we demonstrated that the anti-tubercular clinical candidate (S)-PA-824 possesses moderate activity against L. donovani parasites both in vitro and in vivo (Patterson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Patterson et al., 2013.

claim: (R)-PA-824 showed superior activity compared to (S)-PA-824 against L. donovani.
source: Although (R)-PA-824, the enantiomer of the candidate showed superior activity, this compound has not entered pre-clinical development, precluding a rapid move to a VL clinical trial.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation in the previous sentence to Patterson et al., 2013.

claim: DNDI-VL-2098 was identified as a suitable compound for further preclinical evaluation against L. donovani.
source: In addition, a recently reported screen of anti-tubercular nitroimidazoles against L. donovani identified DNDI-VL-2098 as a suitable compound for further preclinical evaluation (Mukkavilli et al., 2014; Gupta et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mukkavilli et al., 2014 and Gupta et al., 2015.

claim: Delamanid has recently received conditional approval in Europe for the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.
source: The high degree of structural similarity between delamanid (Deltyba, OPC-67683) and both (R)-PA-824 and DNDI-VL-2098 (Figure 1) prompted us to investigate this nitroimidazole, which has recently received conditional approval in Europe for the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, 2013; Ryan and Lo, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, 2013 and Ryan and Lo, 2014.

claim: The (S)-enantiomer of delamanid showed EC50 values of 147 ± 4 nM against L. donovani promastigotes and 1332 ± 106 nM against intracellular amastigotes.
source: The (S)-enantiomer of delamanid showed promising anti-leishmanial activity against both developmental stages of the parasite (EC50 values of 147 ± 4 and 1332 ± 106 nM against promastigotes and amastigotes, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Delamanid (R-enantiomer) showed EC50 values of 15.5 nM against promastigotes, 5.4 nM against axenic amastigotes, and 86.5 nM against intracellular amastigotes.
source: However, delamanid (the R-enantiomer) proved to be an order of magnitude more potent against promastigotes, axenic amastigotes and intracellular amastigotes with EC50 values of 15.5, 5.4 and 86.5 nM, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Table 1.

claim: Both (S)-delamanid and delamanid were found to be inactive (EC50 >50 µM) against the mammalian cell line HepG2.
source: Both compounds were found to be inactive (EC50 >50 µM) in a counter screen against the mammalian cell line HepG2 (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Table 1.

claim: Delamanid is an order of magnitude more potent than (S)-delamanid against L. donovani.
source: However, delamanid (the R-enantiomer) proved to be an order of magnitude more potent against promastigotes, axenic amastigotes and intracellular amastigotes with EC50 values of 15.5, 5.4 and 86.5 nM, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of EC50 values presented in the text and Table 1.

claim: L. donovani clinical isolates were marginally less sensitive to delamanid than the laboratory strain LV9, varying by only 3-fold (L. donovani) or 8-fold (L. infantum) at the EC90.
source: These clinical isolates were marginally less sensitive to delamanid than our laboratory strain LV9 from Ethiopia, but at the EC90 varied by only 3-fold (L. donovani) or 8-fold (L. infantum) (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Table 1.

claim: L. major Friedlin promastigotes were highly sensitive to delamanid with an EC50 of 6.3 ± 0.11 nM.
source: Although not investigated further here, promastigotes of L. major Friedlin, a cause of cutaneous leishmaniasis, were also highly sensitive to delamanid (EC50 6.3 ± 0.11 nM, slope factor 2.2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the text.

claim: Des-nitro-delamanid was found to be inactive (EC50 >50 µM) against L. donovani promastigotes.
source: Des-nitro-delamanid was found to be inactive (EC50 >50 µM), which is consistent with the nitro group being involved in the mechanism of action or having a role in the binding of delamanid to its molecular target(s) in L. donovani.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the text.

claim: The nitro group is involved in the mechanism of action or has a role in the binding of delamanid to its molecular target(s) in L. donovani.
source: Des-nitro-delamanid was found to be inactive (EC50 >50 µM), which is consistent with the nitro group being involved in the mechanism of action or having a role in the binding of delamanid to its molecular target(s) in L. donovani.
evidence: This is an inference based on the inactivity of des-nitro-delamanid.

claim: The plasma protein binding of delamanid was measured and found to be high (Fu = 0.0045).
source: The plasma protein binding of delamanid was measured and found to be high (Fu = 0.0045), in agreement with that reported previously (Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, 2013.

claim: Delamanid possesses sufficient aqueous solubility (>250 µM in 2.5% DMSO) for use in in vitro assays.
source: A kinetic solubility assay demonstrated that delamanid possesses sufficient aqueous solubility (>250 µM in 2.5% DMSO) for use in in vitro assays.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from a kinetic solubility assay.

claim: Twice-daily oral dosing of delamanid at 30 mg kg-1 for 5 days resulted in sterile cures in a mouse model of VL.
source: Twice-daily oral dosing of delamanid at 30 mg kg-1 for 5 days resulted in sterile cures in a mouse model of VL.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo studies.

claim: Treatment with delamanid at 50 mg kg-1 effectively cured the study mice, with no detectable parasites in the liver smears.
source: An initial experiment showed that treatment with delamanid at 50 mg kg-1 effectively cured the study mice, with no detectable parasites in the liver smears, whereas control mice dosed with vehicle alone showed a high level of infection (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Delamanid at 30, 10 or 3 mg kg-1 suppressed infection in the murine model by 99.5%, 63.5% and 16.0%, respectively.
source: A second in vivo study with mice dosed twice-daily at 30, 10 or 3 mg kg-1 suppressed infection in the murine model by 99.5%, 63.5% and 16.0%, respectively, establishing a dose-dependent anti-leishmanial effect within the range of 3–50 mg kg-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo studies.

claim: The estimated ED50 and ED90 of delamanid are 7.3 and 21.5 mg kg-1, respectively.
source: These results give an estimated ED50 and ED90 of 7.3 and 21.5 mg kg-1, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: At 30 and 50 mg kg-1 delamanid compares favourably with miltefosine (98.8–99.8% suppression at 30 mg kg-1).
source: At 30 and 50 mg kg-1 delamanid compares favourably with miltefosine (98.8–99.8% suppression at 30 mg kg-1), which exemplifies the therapeutic potential of delamanid.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing delamanid and miltefosine.

claim: Treatment with lower doses of delamanid revealed a U-shaped (hormetic) dose-response curve with greater parasite suppression at 1 mg kg-1 than at 3 mg kg-1 (5 or 10 day dosing).
source: Treatment with lower doses revealed a U-shaped (hormetic) dose-response curve with greater parasite suppression at 1 mg kg-1 than at 3 mg kg-1 (5 or 10 day dosing).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo studies.

claim: Dosing delamanid for 10 days confirmed the hormetic dose-response and improved the efficacy at all doses investigated.
source: Dosing delamanid for 10 days confirmed the hormetic dose-response and improved the efficacy at all doses investigated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo studies.

claim: A third in vivo study with delamanid at 1 mg kg-1 resulted in a suppression of parasitaemia of 86.3% compared with control mice.
source: A third in vivo study with a further reduced delamanid dose of 1 mg kg-1 resulted in a suppression of parasitaemia of 86.3% compared with control mice, proving unexpectedly superior to dosing at 3 or 10 mg kg-1 (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Delamanid dosed twice-daily for 10 days at 10, 3 or 1 mg kg-1 resulted in suppression of infection of 92.3%, 24.3% and >99.9%, respectively.
source: The hormetic effect was also observed in an extended dosing experiment in which delamanid was instead dosed twice-daily for 10 days at 10, 3 or 1 mg kg-1, with the suppression of infection being 92.3%, 24.3% and >99.9%, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo studies.

claim: Delamanid shows dose linearity up to 10 mg kg-1 and accumulation with repeated administration in mice.
source: Delamanid is orally bioavailable, well tolerated, shows dose linearity up to 10 mg kg-1 and accumulation with repeated administration in agreement with previous pharmacokinetic (PK) studies in mice (Matsumoto et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Matsumoto et al., 2006.

claim: Delamanid is orally bioavailable and well tolerated in mice.
source: Delamanid is orally bioavailable, well tolerated, shows dose linearity up to 10 mg kg-1 and accumulation with repeated administration in agreement with previous pharmacokinetic (PK) studies in mice (Matsumoto et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo studies.

claim: The 10 and 30 mg kg-1 doses of delamanid should provide adequate coverage over the EC90 (120 ng ml-1) as measured for the L. donovani isolate LV9 in macrophages over a 3 day exposure.
source: The 10 and 30 mg kg-1 doses should provide adequate coverage over the EC90 (120 ng ml-1) as measured for the L. donovani isolate LV9 in macrophages over a 3 day exposure (Table 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on pharmacokinetic data and EC90 values from Table 1.

claim: Due to high protein binding (Fu = 0.0045), the free fraction of delamanid cannot account for biological activity in vivo at any dose.
source: However, due to high protein binding, the free fraction (Fu = 0.0045) cannot account for biological activity in vivo at any dose.
evidence: This is an inference based on pharmacokinetic data and protein binding measurements.

claim: Delamanid is rapidly leishmanicidal.
source: No viable parasites could be recovered after 12 hr in the presence of drug, confirming that delamanid is rapidly leishmanicidal.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell killing assays.

claim: Growth of drug-treated L. donovani promastigote cultures ceased almost immediately with cell numbers declining after 8 hr and no live parasites visible at 24 hr when exposed to delamanid at 10 times the EC50 value.
source: Growth of drug-treated cultures ceased almost immediately with cell numbers declining after 8 hr and no live parasites visible at 24 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No viable L. donovani parasites could be recovered after 12 hr in the presence of delamanid.
source: No viable parasites could be recovered after 12 hr in the presence of drug, confirming that delamanid is rapidly leishmanicidal.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell killing assays.

claim: EC50 values of delamanid determined after 24, 48 and 72 hr were essentially identical.
source: In support of this apparent rapid mechanism of cell killing, EC50 values determined after 24, 48 and 72 hr were essentially identical (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The potency (EC50 value) of delamanid was found to be dependent on the initial cell density.
source: In addition, the potency (EC50 value) of delamanid was found to be dependent on the initial cell density (Figure 4C) and on the assay serum concentration (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The potency (EC50 value) of delamanid was found to be dependent on the assay serum concentration.
source: In addition, the potency (EC50 value) of delamanid was found to be dependent on the initial cell density (Figure 4C) and on the assay serum concentration (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In Mycobacterium tuberculosis, delamanid is assumed to be reductively activated by the deazaflavin (F420)-dependent nitroreductase (Ddn).
source: In Mycobacterium tuberculosis, delamanid is assumed to be reductively activated by the same unusual deazaflavin (F420)-dependent nitroreductase (Ddn) known to activate the closely related nitroimidazo-oxazine drug PA-824 (Manjunatha et al., 2006; Singh et al., 2008; Manjunatha et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Manjunatha et al., 2006; Singh et al., 2008; Manjunatha et al., 2009.

claim: Overexpression of NTR in L. donovani promastigotes did not significantly alter their sensitivity to delamanid (EC50 of 4.5 ± 0.004 and 4.1 ± 0.003 nM for WT and transgenic parasites, respectively).
source: However, overexpression of NTR in promastigotes did not significantly alter their sensitivity to delamanid (EC50 of 4.5 ± 0.004 and 4.1 ± 0.003 nM for WT and transgenic parasites, respectively) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Intracellular amastigotes overexpressing NTR were found to be just as sensitive to delamanid as WT parasites with EC50 values of 57.8 ± 2.1 and 55.2 ± 4.3 nM, respectively.
source: The resulting intracellular parasites were found to be just as sensitive to delamanid as WT parasites with EC50 values of 57.8 ± 2.1 and 55.2 ± 4.3 nM, respectively (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: NTR does not play a role in the activation of delamanid in L. donovani in either stage of the life cycle.
source: These findings indicate that NTR does not play a role in the activation of delamanid in L. donovani in either stage of the life cycle and that the mechanism of action of this nitroheterocyclic drug is different from that of fexinidazole.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing no change in sensitivity with NTR overexpression.

claim: The mechanism of action of delamanid is different from that of fexinidazole.
source: These findings indicate that NTR does not play a role in the activation of delamanid in L. donovani in either stage of the life cycle and that the mechanism of action of this nitroheterocyclic drug is different from that of fexinidazole.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing different enzyme requirements for activation.

claim: Delamanid is rapidly metabolised by L. donovani parasites via an enzyme distinct from the nitroreductase that activates fexinidazole.
source: Mechanistic studies reveal that delamanid is rapidly metabolised by parasites via an enzyme, distinct from the nitroreductase that activates fexinidazole.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from metabolism studies and NTR overexpression experiments.

claim: In the presence of L. donovani promastigotes, the rate of disappearance of delamanid was markedly increased, such that the drug had essentially disappeared by 6 hr.
source: However, in the presence of L. donovani promastigotes the rate of disappearance of delamanid was markedly increased, such that the drug had essentially disappeared by 6 hr (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The net amount of delamanid metabolised by L. donovani parasites as a function of time is linear and dependent on the initial concentration in the medium.
source: The net amount of delamanid metabolised by parasites as a function of time is also linear and dependent on the initial concentration in the medium (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The rate of delamanid metabolism by L. donovani is not saturated up to 150 nM.
source: Linear regression of these data revealed that the rate of cell metabolism is not saturated up to the top concentration tested (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Mouse peritoneal macrophages and THP-1 monocytes showed no evidence of delamanid metabolism.
source: Analogous experiments using mouse peritoneal macrophages and THP-1 monocytes found no evidence of delamanid metabolism by these host cell lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from metabolism studies.

claim: Delamanid is highly active in vitro against intracellular L. donovani amastigotes (EC50 0.087 µM).
source: In the current study, we show that delamanid is highly active in vitro against intracellular L. donovani amastigotes (EC50 0.087 µM) with activity superior to that of both the current VL drug miltefosine (EC50 3.3 µM) and the active sulfone metabolite of the VL clinical candidate fexinidazole (EC50 5.3 µM) in the same assay (Wyllie et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Wyllie et al., 2012 for comparison compounds.

claim: Delamanid has activity superior to that of miltefosine (EC50 3.3 µM) against intracellular L. donovani amastigotes.
source: In the current study, we show that delamanid is highly active in vitro against intracellular L. donovani amastigotes (EC50 0.087 µM) with activity superior to that of both the current VL drug miltefosine (EC50 3.3 µM) and the active sulfone metabolite of the VL clinical candidate fexinidazole (EC50 5.3 µM) in the same assay (Wyllie et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing EC50 values.

claim: Delamanid has activity superior to that of the active sulfone metabolite of fexinidazole (EC50 5.3 µM) against intracellular L. donovani amastigotes.
source: In the current study, we show that delamanid is highly active in vitro against intracellular L. donovani amastigotes (EC50 0.087 µM) with activity superior to that of both the current VL drug miltefosine (EC50 3.3 µM) and the active sulfone metabolite of the VL clinical candidate fexinidazole (EC50 5.3 µM) in the same assay (Wyllie et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Wyllie et al., 2012.

claim: The in vitro anti-leishmanial activity of delamanid shows the same enantiomeric specificity as the delamanid analogue DNDI-VL-2098 in vivo.
source: The in vitro anti-leishmanial activity of delamanid shows the same enantiomeric specificity as the delamanid analogue DNDI-VL-2098 in vivo (Gupta et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gupta et al., 2015.

claim: The R-enantiomer of an analogue of delamanid has been shown to be more potent against M. tuberculosis than its corresponding S-enantiomer.
source: Similarly, the R-enantiomer of an analogue of delamanid has been shown to be more potent against M. tuberculosis than its corresponding S-enantiomer (Sasaki et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sasaki et al., 2006.

claim: The enantiomeric specificity of PA-824 for L. donovani and M. tuberculosis is opposite.
source: However, this contrasts with the closely related nitroimidazole PA-824, where the enantiomeric specificity for L. donovani and M. tuberculosis is opposite (Patterson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Patterson et al., 2013.

claim: The observed shift in drug sensitivity with increasing serum concentration is likely due to increased metabolism by albumin to inactive metabolites, rather than changes in free drug concentration due to protein binding.
source: The observed shift in drug sensitivity with increasing serum concentration is likely due to increased metabolism by albumin to inactive metabolites, rather than changes in free drug concentration due to protein binding.
evidence: This is speculation based on known albumin metabolism of delamanid.

claim: The efficacy of delamanid in the VL animal model is unexpected based on the free drug hypothesis.
source: Based on the in vitro intra–macrophage amastigote EC90 value (120 ng ml-1), the high PPB of delamanid (Fu 0.0045) results in an adjusted intra macrophage L. donovani EC90 of 26,700 ng ml-1, a concentration that is not achieved in whole blood at any point in the efficacy study. Therefore, the efficacy of delamanid in the VL animal model is unexpected.
evidence: This is an inference based on pharmacokinetic data and protein binding measurements.

claim: There are exceptions to the free drug theory, such as drugs that form active metabolites resulting in inactivation (covalent or otherwise) of multiple targets.
source: However, there are exceptions to the free drug theory, such as drugs that form active metabolites resulting in inactivation (covalent or otherwise) of multiple targets (Smith et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2010.

claim: The parasite-specific metabolism of delamanid is consistent with exceptions to the free drug theory.
source: The parasite-specific metabolism presented here is entirely consistent with this exception.
evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolism data and knowledge of exceptions to free drug theory.

claim: The U-shaped dose-response curve of delamanid in vivo is reminiscent of hormesis in toxicology.
source: This U-shaped dose-response curve is reminiscent of hormesis in toxicology (Calabrese and Baldwin, 2003; 2002), but, to our knowledge, is unprecedented in microbiology.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Calabrese and Baldwin, 2003; 2002.

claim: The U-shaped dose-response curve of delamanid is unprecedented in microbiology.
source: This U-shaped dose-response curve is reminiscent of hormesis in toxicology (Calabrese and Baldwin, 2003; 2002), but, to our knowledge, is unprecedented in microbiology.
evidence: This is a knowledge claim based on the authors' understanding of the field.

claim: The hormetic effect of delamanid is not observed in dose response curves in vitro, so must be related to a physiological or metabolic threshold response in the infected drug-treated animal.
source: This effect is not observed in dose response curves in vitro, so must be related to a physiological or metabolic threshold response in the infected drug-treated animal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the difference between in vitro and in vivo observations.

claim: In vivo delamanid is proposed to undergo primary metabolism with loss of the nitro group, mainly catalysed by albumin.
source: In vivo delamanid is proposed to undergo primary metabolism with loss of the nitro group, mainly catalysed by albumin (Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, 2013; Shimokawa et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, 2013 and Shimokawa et al., 2015.

claim: Further metabolism of delamanid to seven other metabolites is thought to occur via hydrolysis reactions and oxidation by CYP3A4.
source: Further metabolism to seven other metabolites is thought to occur via hydrolysis reactions and oxidation by CYP3A4 (Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, 2013; Sasahara et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, 2013 and Sasahara et al., 2015.

claim: One possibility for the U-shaped dose-response curve is that a drug metabolite of delamanid antagonises the bio-activation of delamanid, or antagonises the downstream effects in the leishmania parasite.
source: One possibility is that a drug metabolite of delamanid antagonises the bio-activation of delamanid, or antagonises the downstream effects in the leishmania parasite.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of the hormetic effect.

claim: In the same VL animal model, (S)-PA-824 was more efficacious at a lower dose (30 vs 100 mg kg-1).
source: It should be noted that in the same VL animal model the related nitroimidazole (S)-PA-824 was also more efficacious at a lower dose (30 vs 100 mg kg-1) (Patterson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Patterson et al., 2013.

claim: Increasing the dosing duration in the in vivo VL model from 5 to 10 days improved the mean parasite suppression at all investigated doses.
source: Increasing the dosing duration in the in vivo VL model from 5 to 10 days improved the mean parasite suppression at all investigated doses (Figure 2) and resulted in some mice with no detectable liver parasites when dosed at 1 mg kg-1 (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: Delamanid is tolerated for up to six months in TB patients.
source: As it known that delamanid is tolerated for up to six months (Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, 2013) further extending the duration of the VL model beyond 10 days should be considered.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, 2013.

claim: The VL target product profile calls for a treatment regimen of <10 days.
source: The VL target product profile calls for a treatment regimen of <10 days.
evidence: This is knowledge about the VL target product profile.

claim: In the current VL therapy, miltefosine is dosed orally for 28 days.
source: However, in the current VL therapy, miltefosine is dosed orally for 28 days, so extended dosing should be clinically acceptable.
evidence: This is established knowledge about current VL therapy.

claim: The divergent modes of action for fexinidazole and delamanid are advantageous, as the likelihood of cross-resistance developing is reduced.
source: In terms of drug development the divergent modes of action for fexinidazole and delamanid are advantageous, as the likelihood of cross-resistance developing is reduced, and the potential for their co-administration as a combination therapy is retained.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different mechanisms of action.

claim: The divergent modes of action for fexinidazole and delamanid retain the potential for their co-administration as a combination therapy.
source: In terms of drug development the divergent modes of action for fexinidazole and delamanid are advantageous, as the likelihood of cross-resistance developing is reduced, and the potential for their co-administration as a combination therapy is retained.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different mechanisms of action.

claim: Preclinical studies have demonstrated that delamanid is not mutagenic.
source: Preclinical studies have demonstrated that delamanid is not mutagenic (Matsumoto et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Matsumoto et al., 2006.

claim: Repeated oral administration of delamanid in mice or rats for up to 104 weeks showed no evidence of carcinogenicity.
source: Moreover, repeated oral administration in mice or rats for up to 104 weeks showed no evidence of carcinogenicity (Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, 2013.

claim: Thompson and co-workers observed partial efficacy in L. infantum-infected hamsters dosed with delamanid.
source: While revising this manuscript, Thompson and co-workers reported the structure-activity relationships for an extensive series of bicyclic nitro-compounds, including delamanid (Thompson et al., 2016). These authors observed partial efficacy in L. infantum-infected hamsters dosed with delamanid, not inconsistent with our findings.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thompson et al., 2016.

claim: The lower efficacy observed by Thompson and co-workers could be due to inadequate dosing (once versus twice per day), different animal model (hamster versus mouse), or different species of leishmania (L. infantum is less sensitive than L. donovani).
source: The lower efficacy observed by these authors could be due to one or more of the following: inadequate dosing (once versus twice per day); different animal model (hamster versus mouse); or different species of leishmania (L. infantum is less sensitive than L. donovani).
evidence: This is speculation about reasons for differences in efficacy between studies.

claim: Pre-clinical development of VL-2098 has been abandoned due to testicular toxicity.
source: Although this paper found VL-2098 to have superior efficacy in a once daily treatment regimen, pre-clinical development of this compound has been abandoned due to testicular toxicity (http://www.dndi.org/diseases-projects/portfolio/completed-projects/vl-2098/ last accessed 3rd April 2016).
evidence: This is knowledge from a cited web source.

claim: Reproductive toxicity has not been observed with delamanid.
source: Importantly, this reproductive toxicity has not been observed with delamanid (Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, 2013.

claim: Delamanid is rapidly cytocidal.
source: It is rapidly cytocidal and thus potentially efficacious in immunocompromised patients such as those co-infected with HIV (Alvar et al., 2008) particularly since delamanid is not associated with any clinically relevant anti-retroviral drug-drug interactions (Ryan and Lo, 2014; Blair and Scott, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell killing assays.

claim: Delamanid is potentially efficacious in immunocompromised patients such as those co-infected with HIV.
source: It is rapidly cytocidal and thus potentially efficacious in immunocompromised patients such as those co-infected with HIV (Alvar et al., 2008) particularly since delamanid is not associated with any clinically relevant anti-retroviral drug-drug interactions (Ryan and Lo, 2014; Blair and Scott, 2015).
evidence: This is speculation based on the rapid cytocidal activity and lack of drug-drug interactions, with supporting citations.

claim: Delamanid is not associated with any clinically relevant anti-retroviral drug-drug interactions.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ryan and Lo, 2014 and Blair and Scott, 2015.

claim: The VL target product profile specifies that any new treatments should be compatible with TB medications.
source: Due to the prevalence of TB-VL coinfection in Ethiopia (Hurissa et al., 2010) and Sudan (El-Safi et al., 2004) the TPP also specifies that any new treatments should be compatible with TB medications, a stipulation met by delamanid (Blair and Scott, 2015).
evidence: This is knowledge about the VL target product profile, with supporting citations about TB-VL coinfection.

claim: Delamanid is compatible with TB medications.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Blair and Scott, 2015.

claim: Delamanid can be administered orally.
source: Delamanid can be administered orally, an important requirement for patients who have limited access to even the most basic of health care facilities, whereas liposomal amphotericin B (AmBisome) has to be administered intravenously and requires cold storage for stability.
evidence: This is established knowledge about delamanid's route of administration.

claim: The predicted cost per patient for delamanid treatment would be over US$840, assuming an efficacious dose of 100 mg once-daily for in excess of 10 days and the market cost of delamanid in developed countries (US$42 per 50 mg tablet).
source: Assuming an efficacious dose of 100 mg once-daily for in excess of 10 days and the market cost of delamanid in developed countries (US$42 per 50 mg tablet) (Lessem, 2014), the predicted cost per patient would be over US$840, significantly higher than that specified in the VL TPP (<US$10 or <$80 per course) and predicted to be more expensive than other current treatment strategies (Meheus et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on dosing assumptions and market cost data, with supporting citations.

claim: Miltefosine at 30 mg kg-1 once-daily for 5 days resulted in 98.8–99.8% suppression of infection in the mouse VL model.
source: At 30 and 50 mg kg-1 delamanid compares favourably with miltefosine (98.8–99.8% suppression at 30 mg kg-1), which exemplifies the therapeutic potential of delamanid.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo studies.

claim: A 10-day experiment with delamanid at doses of 30, 10, 3, 1, 0.3 mg kg-1 confirmed the hormetic effect.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo studies.

claim: Reducing the delamanid dose to 0.3 mg kg-1 resulted in a reduction in efficacy comparable to dosing at 3 mg kg-1, resulting in a biphasic dose response relationship.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: There is a linear relationship between doses of 0.3–10 mg kg-1 and peak blood concentration (Cmax) or area under the curve (AUC(0-t)) with accumulation from day 1 through to day 10.

claim: Delamanid with a 5 day exposure with daily drug and medium change gave an EC50 value of 28.0 ± 1.6 nM (slope 2.7) from which an EC90 could be calculated (62.7 nM or 33.5 ng ml-1).
source: Given that delamanid is rapidly metabolised by leishmania-infected macrophages in vitro, we examined the effect of delamanid with a 5 day exposure with daily drug and medium change. This gave an EC50 value of 28.0 ± 1.6 nM (slope 2.7) from which an EC90 could be calculated (62.7 nM or 33.5 ng ml-1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from extended exposure assays.

claim: The EC90 concentration of 33.5 ng ml-1 from a 5-day exposure assay is lower than the lowest observed Cmax in the efficacy studies.
source: This concentration is lower than the lowest observed Cmax in the efficacy studies (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of EC90 and Cmax values.
